parts: Please read /papers/investigations-5/04_three_regime_heat_flow_dynamics/notes/06_CHAT0001_RESEARCH_SUMMARY_20261027.md, review the research overview and progress file, and describe the status of the project at a high level.
I’ll read the research summary, overview, and progress file, then describe the main results, open questions, and current direction.

The main advance is a stronger bound on where a nonreal zero can be found near time zero. It remains compatible with all three regimes. The response-analysis branch has also identified why one proposed method fails as the observation window grows.

As of **27 October 2026**, the investigation has obtained substantive quantitative analytical results, but **has not yet distinguished which of the three regimes the canonical heat flow occupies**. RH, simplicity, and exclusion of a positive Newman threshold remain open.

The [research overview](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/04_three_regime_heat_flow_dynamics/research-overview/01_THREE_REGIME_DYNAMICS_RESEARCH_OVERVIEW_20261026.md) compares three possibilities:

| Regime | Meaning | Expected behavior just before time zero |
|---|---|---|
| A | RH fails; Newman threshold is positive | Nonreal zeros persist in a bounded region. |
| B | RH holds, with some multiple zeros | Multiple zeros split into nearby nonreal zeros. |
| C | RH holds, with all zeros simple | Nonreal zeros leave every fixed bounded region as time approaches zero. |

The strongest recent advance is the [summary’s quantitative bound](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/04_three_regime_heat_flow_dynamics/notes/06_CHAT0001_RESEARCH_SUMMARY_20261027.md):
\[
R_*(\tau)\le \exp\!\exp\!\left(C_d/\sqrt{\tau}\right),
\qquad 0<\tau\le1,
\]
where \(R_*(\tau)\) is the distance from the origin to the nearest nonreal zero at time \(-\tau\). This improves the earlier double-exponential bound with \(\tau^{-3}\) in the inner exponent. The gain comes from constructing much more tightly localized seed zeros and carrying their estimates through the full approximation and transport argument.

Its significance is a stronger guarantee that a nonreal zero exists within a specified radius. **It supplies neither a lower escape rate nor the actual first-zero location**, and all three regimes satisfy it. The constants also remain unevaluated, so there is no practical numerical location bound yet.

The other main branch studies how an observable detects multiple zeros. It now has an explicit fixed-window response with an \(O(\tau^2)\) remainder and estimates for observation error. Extending this to expanding windows remains unresolved. A separate continuation established that one specified global error-budget method fails for the tested growing-window scales; localized alternatives remain available.

The [progress register](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/04_three_regime_heat_flow_dynamics/research-progress/01_THREE_REGIME_DYNAMICS_RESEARCH_PROGRESS_20261026.md) therefore appropriately marks the quantitative tasks **Partial**. Connecting these results to the full physical equations, excluding a positive threshold, and obtaining an estimate that rules out a regime remain **Open**.

The clearest next steps are to reduce the costly recurrence estimate in the Dobner construction, or certify a concrete seed contour and evaluate the missing constants on a specified interval. The response branch needs a localized estimate that remains effective as the window grows. The larger scientific objective is an independently established constraint from the canonical source that conflicts with one regime’s required behavior.

These results currently have analytical proofs recorded in notes and internal same-model reviews, with no numerical certification or independent specialist review—consistent with the repository’s [status conventions](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/result-summaries/README.md) and [review limitations](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/avoid/05_same_model_reviews_and_shared_premises.md).

I'm starting to understand more deeply why proving \Lambda \geq 0 is easier than proving \Lambda \leq 0. When you assume \Lamda < 0, then the dynamics between \Lambda and 0 between the real zeros force statistical behavior that is detectable at zero, and leads to a contradiction (Rodgers Tao). If you assume \Lambda > 0, then you have less information at t = 0, because RH doesn't hold, so there is less to work with for a contradiction. Also, there is less of a detectable signature of a single collision, vs assuming \Lambda < 0 where the dynamics in that interval affect all of the zeros. Dobner's method also faces difficulties, because the approximation gives non-critical zeros, but approximations at t > 0 would have to be perfect to exclude zeros.
I’ll check this against the project’s Rodgers–Tao and Dobner records, especially the distinction between finding a nonreal zero and excluding all of them.

The records support your point about a single collision escaping bulk statistics. One correction matters: zero exclusion can tolerate nonzero approximation error. The difficulty is proving that the error stays below a suitable margin everywhere needed, especially near a possible collision.

Yes—your account captures the central asymmetry. I would sharpen the role of the time-zero slice and revise the claim that exclusion requires a perfect approximation.

**Assuming \(\Lambda<0\) supplies a powerful extra hypothesis:** a fixed interval of entirely real-zero dynamics *before reaching the original zeta function*. At high heights, the mean spacing becomes small, so that fixed interval contains many local interaction times. This explains the equilibration mechanism: Rodgers–Tao turn it into an averaged rigidity statement at \(t=0\) that contradicts known zeta spacing results. Those RH-dependent results are available because the contradiction hypothesis already implies RH. The conclusion concerns broad statistical behavior, without requiring identical behavior at every individual zero. [Rodgers–Tao](https://arxiv.org/html/1801.05914v5)

Under \(\Lambda=T>0\), we retain all the exact arithmetic information about \(H_0\), but **lose the all-real dynamical interval connecting that information to an equilibrated endpoint**. The available real-zero evolution lies above \(T\), where its regularizing behavior is compatible with positive-time heat deformations. Moving the time origin does not restore the argument: the new endpoint has source \(e^{Tu^2}\Phi(u)\), and its zeros do not automatically inherit the relevant zeta statistics.

Your point about an isolated collision is also consequential. In the canonical family, a positive threshold entails a finite multiple-zero event, but need not force a positive density of such events. A single exceptional collision can disappear from normalized large-height statistics. An averaged argument would therefore need an additional mechanism showing that this local event produces a detectable aggregate effect. The project’s [positive-threshold analysis](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/02_heat_flow_rh_applications/notes/02_RODGERS_TAO_POSITIVE_THRESHOLD_20261026.md) identifies precisely this gap.

Dobner exposes another aspect of the asymmetry:

- To prove \(\Lambda\ge0\), it suffices, at each fixed \(t<0\), to produce **one** nonreal zero.
- To prove \(\Lambda\le0\), one must exclude **every** nonreal zero at \(t=0\), or establish all-real zeros at positive times approaching zero.

A seed zero with a protective contour can survive an imperfect approximation, which makes the existence argument robust. Dobner’s particular series also benefits from the damping factor \(e^{t(\log n)^2/4}\) for \(t<0\); for \(t>0\), that ordinary Dirichlet series diverges, so its representation cannot simply be reused. [Dobner](https://arxiv.org/html/2005.05142v2)

**Exclusion can nevertheless tolerate nonzero error.** If \(H=G+E\), then
\[
|E(z)|<|G(z)|
\]
excludes zeros wherever that inequality holds. On a contour, it preserves the enclosed zero count by Rouché’s theorem. If a conjugation-symmetric disk contains exactly one zero of the real-symmetric function \(H\), that zero must be real. These are exact conclusions obtained from approximate information. Polymath’s proof of \(\Lambda\le0.22\) already demonstrates the usefulness of controlled approximations for upper bounds. [Polymath](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2)

The difficulty is obtaining adequate margins and complete coverage as the target time approaches zero. Near a possible double zero, those margins can collapse: the elementary example \(z^2+\varepsilon\) acquires nonreal zeros for every \(\varepsilon>0\), however small. For our project, this makes the next question more specific: can the canonical arithmetic control the error **relative to the local collision scale**, including exceptional configurations that bulk statistics may miss?

That approach is sound, but I'm concerned that it leads to a numerical journey of increasingly sophisticated approximations, and I'm not sure if the tools that we've developed so far will help significantly there. I'm sure that this route has been tried already by many people in very sophisticated ways, so it will be a difficult journey. 

One tool that seemed to work fairly well that we developed is the hierarchy that we discovered for negative time in 01_heat_density_asymptotics. One question I have about that, why was it so difficult to extend the results to t=0? I think this question may be relevant for the analysis here.
I’ll trace the negative-time hierarchy and the estimates that lose control near \(t=0\), to separate a limitation of the approximation from a change in the underlying zero behavior.

The strongest hierarchy was extended to \(T=-t\ge 1/\log(X/(4\pi))\), but its estimates still lose control below that scale. The underlying field is regular at zero. A specific source of the loss is the Gaussian integral on a fixed complex strip: taking absolute values introduces \(e^{(\Im z)^2/(4T)}\), which grows rapidly as \(T\downarrow0\).

There is also a useful distinction in the record: the earlier work did reach \(t=0\), using a different representation with weaker accuracy. The recurrence organizes gamma-factor corrections while retaining the full arithmetic sum. That helps explain both its success and why extending it would not, by itself, settle the zero-location question.

The difficulty was principally **preserving the hierarchy’s strong, uniform error estimates as \(t\to0\)**. The exact heat-flow function is regular there. And there is an important correction to the premise: **we did obtain a weaker bridge through zero**, using a different representation.

Writing \(T=-t>0\) and \(L=\log(X/(4\pi))\), the recorded results are:

| Construction | What it reaches |
|---|---|
| Negative-time recurrence hierarchy | Error \(e^{-L^2/4}\), relative to its positive comparison envelope, on \(1/L\le T\le2\). |
| Earlier crossover and joined representation | Reaches \(t=0\); field error there is \(O(X^{-3/4})\) relative to its stated envelope, with weaker uniform estimates across the joined interval. |

Thus the unfinished step is carrying the **strong hierarchy and its error control** through zero. The boundary \(T=1/L\) is a proved range, not an established impossibility barrier. [Moving-endpoint result](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/recurrence/notes/20_MOVING_LOWER_ENDPOINT_20261026.md), [through-zero bridge](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/notes/06_NEGATIVE_BRIDGE_AND_TIME_JOIN_20261025.md)

The most concrete obstruction comes from **how we estimated the Gaussian convolution**. For negative time,
\[
H(-T,z)=\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi T}}
\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-(z-u)^2/(4T)}H(0,u)\,du.
\]
This allowed us to use controlled real-axis Riemann–Siegel data to construct a holomorphic approximation. But for \(z=x+iy\),
\[
\left|e^{-(z-u)^2/(4T)}\right|
=e^{y^2/(4T)}e^{-(x-u)^2/(4T)}.
\]

On a fixed complex strip, the factor \(e^{y^2/(4T)}\) becomes enormous as \(T\downarrow0\). Derivative estimates introduce additional inverse powers of \(T\). The exact integral remains well behaved because of cancellations, but taking absolute values loses those cancellations.

This explains the successful moving endpoint: at \(T=1/L\), the transverse loss is only \(e^{O(L)}\), which the available \(e^{-cL^2}\) accuracy can absorb. Sending \(T\) to zero at fixed height destroys that balance. **The blow-up belongs to the estimate; it does not establish a blow-up of the function or an unavoidable computational cost.**

There is a second distinction concerning **what the hierarchy actually organizes**. Its levels describe corrections to the smooth gamma factor, while retaining the full arithmetic sum of roughly \(\sqrt X\) modes. Negative-time evolution supplies mode damping, but even there we did not prove that a few modes determine the signed total. As \(T\) decreases, that damping weakens and the arithmetic interference becomes more exposed.

Indeed, the recurrence operator
\[
\mathcal Q_T=d+2T\partial_d
\]
itself has a perfectly regular limit at \(T=0\). The finite recurrence levels survive algebraically. What needs new treatment is the complete remainder and retained correction integral, uniformly in height and on the required complex neighborhoods. [Hierarchy construction](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/notes/16_GAUSSIAN_FLUCTUATION_HIERARCHY_20261026.md)

That is relevant to your concern about an endless approximation campaign. The Gaussian-convolution/Riemann–Siegel architecture already appears in sophisticated work such as [Polymath’s analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2). Our hierarchy provides an organized analytical expansion and controlled errors; additional orders alone do not establish the arithmetic restrictions needed to prevent collisions.

There is, however, a useful connection to the present investigation. **On the natural collision scale \(y=\sqrt T\,\eta\), the troublesome exponential becomes**
\[
e^{y^2/(4T)}=e^{\eta^2/4},
\]
which no longer grows with \(1/T\). This suggests examining the hierarchy in shrinking neighborhoods adapted to collision dynamics. The analytic buffers and derivative estimates would also have to be redesigned, and the missing arithmetic and root-separation information would remain.

I would therefore distinguish two research questions: improving field accuracy through zero, and extracting an event-sensitive constraint from the hierarchy. The second could exploit its structure without first requiring a large numerical program. The fixed-strip difficulty gives a specific reason to investigate a different observation scale.

Can you dive deeper into that last point about focusing on a natural collision scale and honing in on the troublesome exponential? I think there is a lot to unpack in what you said, and it feels like the seed of something that could lead to a real argument. Can you describe in detail what you meant, and brainstorm about ways that that could lead to a contradiction or some proof mechanism to outlaw collisions at positive t?

I’ll work through the collision rescaling, check which estimates it improves, and examine what additional arithmetic information could turn it into a positive-time collision exclusion. I’ll save the analysis and its limits in the investigation’s notes.

The rescaling does remove the \(e^{C/T}\) loss on suitably shrinking neighborhoods. It also reveals two limits: a collision has the same leading Hermite profile for many heat flows, and its field amplitude shrinks like a power of the observation radius. A potentially useful direction is to make one collision detectable across infinitely many shrinking time scales, then seek a canonical-source estimate that forbids that accumulated signal.

The endpoint-energy route already appears in the project’s earlier analysis, so I’m treating it as an existing target. The sharper connection here is that a collision contributes a fixed positive amount of inverse-gap energy on every shrinking time annulus. That shows how one isolated event could become statistically visible—but the independent arithmetic bound needed to contradict it is still missing.

I’m using the Pages writing guidance for the saved note, with the repository’s existing notes folder as its destination.

For a double collision at \(t_c\), the local model gives gap squared \(8(t-t_c)\). Its inverse-gap energy therefore contributes \(\tfrac18\log4\) on each interval \([t_c+r^2,t_c+4r^2]\). That gives a concrete contradiction target: a bound from the canonical source with a strictly smaller accumulated coefficient. The rescaled approximation can help control errors in such a comparison; it does not yet supply that bound.

The strongest possibility I see is this: **a single collision produces a definite signal on every smaller time scale.** The rescaling could make approximation errors small enough to add across those scales. A contradiction would then require a bound from the actual Riemann heat flow that cannot accommodate the accumulated signal.

That gives a more specific analytical target than progressively improving an approximation. But the source-specific bound is still missing.

Let me separate what the scaling genuinely accomplishes from what a proof would still need.

Suppose there is a collision at positive time \(t_c\), at the real point \(a\), with multiplicity \(m\geq2\). Write
\[
c=\frac{\partial_z^m H(t_c,a)}{m!}\neq0.
\]
For our convention \(H_t=-H_{zz}\), the natural coordinates are
\[
t=t_c+r^2s,\qquad z=a+rw.
\]
Space has scale \(r\); time has scale \(r^2\). After also normalizing the amplitude,
\[
F_r(s,w)=\frac{H(t_c+r^2s,a+rw)}{cr^m},
\]
the local heat equation gives
\[
F_r(s,w)=P_m(s,w)+O(r),\qquad
P_m(s,w)=e^{-s\partial_w^2}w^m.
\]

For a double collision this is simply
\[
P_2(s,w)=w^2-2s.
\]
At scaled time \(s=-1\), the two zeros are \(\pm i\sqrt2\); at \(s=1\), they are \(\pm\sqrt2\). The collision has become an event of fixed size, however small \(r\) is. Higher multiplicities give the corresponding Hermite polynomial profile. This local behavior is established in the heat-flow literature. [Polymath, Proposition 3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S3)

**This is the scale on which we should examine the troublesome exponential.** The backward comparison from the collision time is
\[
H(t_c-\varepsilon,z)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon}}
\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-(z-u)^2/(4\varepsilon)}H(t_c,u)\,du.
\]
For \(z=x+iy\), taking absolute values introduces
\[
e^{y^2/(4\varepsilon)}.
\]
Keeping \(y\) fixed while \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) creates the enormous loss we discussed. But put
\[
\varepsilon=r^2\theta,\qquad z=a+rw,\qquad u=a+rv.
\]
The kernel becomes
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi\theta}}
e^{-(w-v)^2/(4\theta)}\,dv,
\]
and its complex amplification is now
\[
e^{(\operatorname{Im}w)^2/(4\theta)}.
\]
On a bounded scaled neighborhood, with \(\theta\) bounded away from zero, this is a fixed constant. **The exponential blowup disappears.**

Derivative estimates can benefit too, provided their analytic neighborhoods shrink with \(r\). Using a fixed physical neighborhood for a Cauchy estimate would bring the same problem back.

There are two qualifications. First, \(\varepsilon=t_c-t\) is distance to the hypothetical collision. Our original negative-time hierarchy was based at \(t=0\). Recentring the canonical integral at \(t_c\) changes its source to \(e^{t_cu^2}\Phi(u)\), so the old hierarchy does not automatically carry over. Second, the field itself has size \(|c|r^m\). An approximation must therefore have error small relative to that:
\[
|\text{error}|\ll |c|r^m.
\]
An error that merely tends to zero is insufficient.

Nevertheless, this replaces one severe obstruction with a more natural local requirement: resolve the field relative to the size of the collision.

The next question is what to measure. Here I think there is a particularly useful connection to your observation that one collision seems statistically invisible.

Immediately after a double collision,
\[
x_\pm(t_c+s)=a\pm\sqrt{2s}+O(s),
\]
so
\[
\frac{1}{(x_+(t_c+s)-x_-(t_c+s))^2}
=
\frac{1}{8s}+O(s^{-1/2}).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\int_{r^2}^{4r^2}
\frac{ds}{(x_+(t_c+s)-x_-(t_c+s))^2}
=
\frac18\log4+O(r).
\]

Every successive time interval
\[
[r^2,4r^2],\quad [r^2/4,r^2],\quad [r^2/16,r^2/4],\ldots
\]
contributes essentially the same positive amount.

Thus **one collision is sparse in the population of zeros, but persistent across infinitely many scales.** That is a way of making an isolated event detectable without averaging over all zeros.

The same calculation works for higher multiplicity. For the \(m\) descendants of the collision, define the energy using unordered pairs:
\[
E_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)
=
\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{(x_i(t_c+s)-x_j(t_c+s))^2}.
\]
The Hermite profile gives
\[
E_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)
=
\frac{\kappa_m}{s}+O(s^{-1/2}),
\qquad
\kappa_m=\frac{m(m-1)}{16}.
\]
In particular,
\[
\int_\epsilon^{s_0}E_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\,ds
=
\kappa_m\log\frac{s_0}{\epsilon}+O(1).
\]
The smallest possible coefficient is \(1/8\), attained by a double collision.

This gives a precise conditional contradiction mechanism. Choose a fixed small window around the hypothetical collision and let \(E_W\) include all pairs of real zeros in that window. If the canonical source could independently imply
\[
\int_\epsilon^{s_0}E_W(t_c+s)\,ds
\leq
\vartheta\log\frac{s_0}{\epsilon}+C,
\qquad \vartheta<\frac18,
\]
with \(C\) independent of \(\epsilon\), then the collision would be impossible. A finite integral, or an \(o(\log(1/\epsilon))\) bound, would also suffice.

The independence of \(C\) is essential: it cannot hide a dependence on the smallest gap. Neither analyticity of \(H\) nor ordinary energy dissipation supplies this bound. An analytic function can have merging zeros whose inverse-gap energy diverges exactly this way.

The project’s earlier [Rodgers–Tao threshold analysis](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/02_heat_flow_rh_applications/notes/02_RODGERS_TAO_POSITIVE_THRESHOLD_20261026.md) already identified endpoint energy control as a target. The useful refinement here is the explicit contribution on each scale and its connection to the exponential-loss problem.

This suggests three directions worth distinguishing.

1. **Make hierarchy errors summable across collision scales.**  
   Suppose a source calculation gives an error \(O(r^\alpha)\), with \(\alpha>0\), on the interval \([r^2,4r^2]\). Along geometric scales, those errors have a finite sum. The collision’s contribution has an infinite sum because it contributes a fixed positive amount on every interval.

   This is a concrete role for the hierarchy: establish enough accuracy that errors cannot conceal the accumulated collision signal. It would not require arbitrarily high orders; one positive power of \(r\) could be enough.

   The hard step is identifying the main source expression and proving a bound with a coefficient below the collision coefficient. If the source calculation simply reproduces \(\kappa_m\log4\) on every interval, greater accuracy provides no contradiction.

2. **Use a localized transverse moment just before the collision.**  
   There is a complementary observable on the complex-zero side. Choose a smooth cutoff \(\chi\) that contains the scaled collision cluster and define
   \[
   Y_r=
   \sum_{H(t_c-r^2,z)=0}
   \chi\!\left(\frac{z-a}{r}\right)(\operatorname{Im}z)^2.
   \]
   The local profile forces
   \[
   \frac{Y_r}{r^2}\longrightarrow 2m(m-1)\geq4.
   \]
   A double collision therefore leaves a fixed normalized transverse signal. It is not diluted by the total number of zeros.

   An independent canonical bound
   \[
   \limsup_{r\downarrow0}\frac{Y_r}{r^2}<4
   \]
   would exclude it. This fits the weak-potential machinery developed in the current investigation: the moment can be represented through an integral involving \(\log|H|\), and rescaling makes its error estimates more manageable.

   Again, the key word is *independent*. Assuming a collision and deriving its Hermite profile gives the lower limit above; approximating that same profile cannot give a contradictory upper bound.

3. **Connect the local cluster to the canonical source and the exterior zeros.**  
   Near the event, factor
   \[
   H(t,z)=P(t,z)U(t,z),
   \]
   where \(P\) contains the colliding cluster and \(U\) is nonvanishing locally. The cluster’s leading motion is universal. Any distinguishing information must enter through constraints coupling its coefficients, the exterior factor \(U\), and the original theta source.

   One possible quantity is the cluster discriminant,
   \[
   D(t)=\prod_{i<j}(x_i(t)-x_j(t))^2.
   \]
   Its logarithmic derivative contains \(8E_{\mathrm{cl}}\), together with terms from \(U\). This connects the energy target to the project’s coefficient-transport work, where one can evolve cluster coefficients without introducing internal inverse-gap denominators.

   But replacing the energy by \(\log D\) merely relocates the difficulty unless the canonical source controls the endpoint behavior of \(D\). The needed ingredient would be an actual signed inequality or cancellation, retained before taking absolute values.

That last requirement is where I would concentrate the search. At a double collision, the canonical source satisfies simultaneous oscillatory moment equations of the form
\[
\int_0^\infty e^{t_cu^2}\Phi(u)\cos(au)\,du=0,
\qquad
\int_0^\infty u\,e^{t_cu^2}\Phi(u)\sin(au)\,du=0.
\]
Positivity of \(\Phi\) alone does not prevent these cancellations. The theta structure would have to yield something stronger about their joint behavior, or about the cluster energy they generate.

There is a stringent test for any proposed mechanism: generic heat flows—including positive-source examples—can have positive-time collisions and exhibit exactly the same scaled profile. A successful argument must identify a quantitative canonical inequality those examples fail. Universal heat-flow identities and increasingly accurate local approximations cannot provide that distinction by themselves.

My preference is therefore to pursue the energy formulation first, using the transverse moment as a second way to measure the same event. The immediate analytical task would be to identify a signed source expression that controls the contribution on one time annulus, then determine whether the actual theta structure forces a strict saving. The hierarchy would handle the errors around that comparison.

This need not become an exhaustive numerical search. In an analytic contradiction, we may fix a hypothetical finite collision and take \(r\) sufficiently small; constants can depend on that event. What must hold for every candidate is the independent source inequality.

I saved the detailed derivations, conditional targets, and limitations in [the collision-scale research note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/04_three_regime_heat_flow_dynamics/notes/07_COLLISION_SCALE_RESOLUTION_AND_PROOF_MECHANISMS_20261027.md), with a [separate self-assessment](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/04_three_regime_heat_flow_dynamics/reviews/04_COLLISION_SCALE_MECHANISMS_SELF_ASSESSMENT_20261027.md). The scaling improvement and collision signal are concrete; the canonical inequality needed to turn them into an exclusion remains unproved.

I like the idea that the hierarchy plays the concrete role of bounding the error sufficiently to rule out collisions. This could also lead to partial progress - a lower upper bound for \Lambda. Is this related to the energy formulation? You mentioned possibly having to recenter the hierarchy around the collision, did I read that correctly?
I’ll check how an energy bound above a chosen time could give an upper bound for \(\Lambda\), and clarify what recentering would require from the hierarchy.

The earlier threshold note already identifies a fixed positive-time interval as a route to a smaller upper bound. The key distinction is that shifting the time coordinate is exact, while transferring the negative-time hierarchy’s error theorem requires new estimates for the shifted source. I’m making that distinction explicit in the collision-scale note.

Yes—**a smaller positive upper bound for \(\Lambda\) is a natural intermediate goal**, and the energy formulation gives one way to connect that goal to hierarchy error estimates. And yes, you read the recentering point correctly, with an important distinction: changing the coordinates is exact; extending the hierarchy’s error theorem to those coordinates is new work.

Start with an established upper bound \(\Lambda\le B\), and choose a smaller target \(0<b<B\). We would aim to exclude a threshold collision at every possible time
\[
b<t_c\le B.
\]
For the canonical flow, a positive threshold entails a collision at finite height. Thus excluding those events would establish \(\Lambda\le b\). We would not need to reach zero to obtain a meaningful result.

A fixed \(b>0\) also provides a useful foothold: existing positive-time asymptotics confine possible collisions to a bounded height range, uniformly over a fixed positive-time interval. The theoretical cutoff grows roughly like \(e^{C/b}\), so passing to \(b=0\) remains a separate difficulty. [Polymath, Theorem 1.5](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2)

The connection to energy is that it supplies a **specific signal the error must be too small to conceal**. At a hypothetical collision,
\[
\int_\epsilon^{s_0}E_W(t_c+s)\,ds
\ge
\frac18\log\frac{s_0}{\epsilon}+O(1).
\]
Here \(E_W\) is the unordered inverse-square pair energy in a window containing the event. Higher multiplicity only increases the leading coefficient.

Suppose a source calculation, using an order-\(N\) hierarchy, independently gave
\[
\int_\epsilon^{s_0}E_W(t_c+s)\,ds
\le
\bigl[A_N+\eta_N\bigr]\log\frac{s_0}{\epsilon}+C_N,
\]
where:

- \(A_N\) is the coefficient furnished by the main source calculation;
- \(\eta_N\) is the complete error allowance affecting that coefficient;
- \(C_N\) is independent of the lower cutoff \(\epsilon\) and of any assumed minimum gap.

Then
\[
A_N+\eta_N<\frac18
\]
would exclude the collision. If that inequality could be established for every candidate above \(b\), it would prove \(\Lambda\le b\).

**This is where improved hierarchy estimates could buy a smaller upper bound:** reducing \(\eta_N\) might let the inequality remain valid at smaller positive times. But the main source calculation must supply a margin in the first place. Higher accuracy alone cannot make a coefficient exceeding \(1/8\) fall below it.

There is a useful refinement here. On the successive collision scales \(r,r/2,r/4,\ldots\):

- An error \(O(r^\alpha)\), with \(\alpha>0\), has a finite total. It contributes only to the bounded term \(C_N\).
- An error that stays roughly constant on each scale accumulates logarithmically. It contributes to \(\eta_N\).

That tells us what to ask of the hierarchy. We want to identify which errors alter the leading logarithmic coefficient and which can be made summable. Once an error is summable, making it dramatically smaller may add nothing to the contradiction.
